title: The mother sauces
intro: Béchamel, velouté, espagnole, tomato and hollandaise, and the small sauces each one gives. Learn the liaison and the liquid of each mother, and the family tree follows.

entries.title: The idea of the mother sauces
entries.summary: A mother sauce is a base that many smaller sauces grow from. Carême named four, Escoffier's Guide of 1903 named four of its own, and later schools taught five. Learn the liquid and the thickener of each, and the family follows.
entries.guest: Most classic French sauces grow from a handful of mother sauces. Ours lean on the hollandaise family, warm, buttery and bright, with a red wine sauce, marchand de vin, on the Eggs Hussarde.

paras: A mother sauce is a base sauce, made in quantity and kept ready, from which many smaller sauces are built. The cook takes a ladle of the mother and adds something to it: a flavour such as wine, mustard or herbs, a garnish such as mushrooms or capers, or an enrichment such as cream, egg yolk or butter. The French call the results petites sauces, small sauces, and English kitchens often call them daughters. One well-made mother can become a dozen sauces in a single service, which is why a classical kitchen is organised around a few of them.
Every mother is defined by two things: its liquid and what thickens it. Learn those two for each one and you can place almost any classical sauce on the family tree.

The idea was set down by Marie-Antoine Carême, the Paris chef who shaped grand French cooking in the early nineteenth century. He sorted sauces into families headed by four: espagnole, velouté, allemande and béchamel. In his scheme allemande, a velouté bound with egg yolk, still counted as a parent in its own right.

Auguste Escoffier revised the list in Le Guide culinaire, first published in 1903. His grandes sauces de base, the great base sauces, are four: espagnole, velouté, béchamel and tomate. Demi-glace and allemande stand close beside them as working bases, drawn from espagnole and velouté, and hollandaise appears among the small sauces that follow, not among the bases.

The tidy list of five mother sauces, with hollandaise promoted to sit beside the four, is later teaching. The English translation of 1907, A Guide to Modern Cookery, prints hollandaise in its chapter of leading warm sauces, and many trace the five to that page; twentieth-century cookery schools and textbooks then made the five the standard lesson. Learn the five, and know that Escoffier's French book names four.

The five, by liquid and thickener. Béchamel is milk thickened with a white roux, flour cooked in butter without colour. Velouté is white stock, from veal, chicken or fish, thickened with a blond roux, cooked to pale straw. Espagnole is brown stock, made from roasted bones, thickened with a brown roux. Tomate is tomatoes cooked slowly with pork, aromatics and white stock, thickened by reduction, and in Escoffier's version by a little roux as well. Hollandaise is egg yolk and butter held as an emulsion, a sauce in which tiny droplets of fat stay suspended in a little water.
Mayonnaise stands beside them as the cold emulsion: egg yolk and oil, whisked together raw, and the parent of many cold sauces, rémoulade among them.

On the floor this is a shortcut. Name the mother and most questions about a sauce answer themselves: what it is built on, how rich it eats, whether it is bright or deep, and which wine will meet it. A daughter of hollandaise is buttery and bright with lemon or vinegar; a daughter of espagnole is dark and meaty. A guest's question about allergies still goes to the kitchen every time, because a small sauce can carry more than its mother.

Brennan's menus read like a lesson in the hollandaise family: plain hollandaise on the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen, béarnaise on the breakfast Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak, Choron on the Eggs Sardou and Foyot on the Roasted Chateaubriand. The marchand de vin beneath the egg on the Hussarde and the Owen comes from the brown side. The house study card asks for the five mother sauces: give the five, and if a guest is curious, tell how the list grew from Carême's four, through the four base sauces of Escoffier's Guide, to the schools' five.

brennans.how: The Hussarde puts two families on one plate: hollandaise, the yolk and butter mother, and marchand de vin, a red wine sauce from the brown side. Name both mothers and the plate explains itself.

The Sardou carries Choron, béarnaise finished with tomato cooked down to a thick paste, so it belongs to the hollandaise family: yolk and butter first, then tarragon, then tomato for colour and a gentle sweetness.
The Chateaubriand carries sauce Foyot, béarnaise with meat glaze whisked in: a daughter of the hollandaise line given savoury depth from the brown side, which suits the lean, mild tenderloin.

entries.title: Béchamel
entries.summary: Béchamel is milk thickened with a white roux and seasoned with salt, white pepper and nutmeg. It is the gentlest mother sauce and the first one a cook learns, the base of gratins, croquettes and soufflés.
entries.guest: Béchamel is a creamy white sauce of milk thickened with butter and flour, with a little nutmeg. It is the sauce behind a classic gratin or croque monsieur.

paras: Béchamel is milk thickened with a white roux: flour cooked in butter just long enough to lose its raw edge, but never coloured. It is seasoned with salt, white pepper, which keeps the sauce pale with no dark specks, and a grating of nutmeg. It is mild, milky and smooth, a carrier for whatever is added to it.

It matters because so much rests on it. Thin, it starts cream soups; at coating weight it goes over vegetables, eggs and fish for gratins; thick, it binds croquettes and makes the base of a savoury soufflé. Add cheese, onion or cream and it becomes a family of small sauces of its own.

Butter and flour go in equal weights, and the amount of roux sets the thickness. For 1 litre (about 1 quart) of milk, a thin béchamel takes about 30 g (1 oz) each of butter and flour and pours freely. A medium one takes about 60 g (2 oz) of each and coats the back of a spoon. A thick one takes 90 to 100 g (about 3.5 oz) of each and holds its shape, ready to bind croquettes or a soufflé base.

The classical build starts with an onion piqué: half an onion with a bay leaf pinned to it by a clove or two. Warm the milk with the onion in it and leave it to infuse for about 10 minutes while you make the roux; some cooks simmer the onion in the finished sauce instead, and either way it comes out. Some old versions cooked a little lean veal in the sauce or loosened it with white stock, but most kitchens today keep it to milk.

Melt the butter over a low heat, stir in the flour and cook for 2 to 3 minutes, stirring, until it smells of biscuit rather than raw flour but shows no colour. Add the warm milk in three or four stages, whisking each one smooth before the next. The first addition seizes into a thick paste, and that is right. Keep whisking as it comes up to a bare simmer and thickens.

Now cook it out. Keep it at a gentle simmer for at least 15 to 20 minutes, stirring the bottom and corners of the pan, until no floury taste remains. Season, then strain through a fine sieve. To stop a skin forming, press baking parchment or cling film onto the surface, or dot the top with butter. Hold it in a bain-marie, a pan set in hot water, at 57°C (135°F) or above, the hot-holding line in the FDA Food Code.

Lumps come from adding the milk too fast, or from milk and roux that are both very hot, so the starch swells before it can spread. The rule is cool or warm milk into a hot roux, or hot milk into a cooled roux, a little at a time; a lumpy sauce can be whisked hard and passed through a fine sieve. Scorching comes from too much heat and too little stirring. Pour the sauce into a clean pan without scraping, taste it, and start again if it is bitter. A raw, pasty taste means it was not cooked long enough: keep simmering.

The name is tied by tradition to Louis de Béchameil, steward of the household to Louis XIV. Nobody has shown that he made the sauce or asked for it, so tell it as a story the French kitchen tells about itself, not as fact.

The house notes describe creamed spinach as spinach blanched, squeezed hard and chopped, then bound with reduced cream or a light béchamel. Which binding the kitchen uses for the Brennan's Creamed Spinach side, and whether the sauce carries flour, is confirmed at lineup before you say so.

To a guest, béchamel is a creamy white sauce of milk thickened with butter and flour, with a hint of nutmeg. It is not cream, though it eats like it, and it is not a cheese sauce until cheese goes in. A guest who asks what is in a dish, or whether milk or flour is part of it, gets the kitchen's answer, never a guess.

questions.q: What kind of roux thickens a béchamel?
questions.answer: A white roux, cooked without colour
distractors: A brown roux, cooked to hazelnut
A blond roux, cooked to pale straw
No roux at all, only egg yolk
questions.why: Béchamel takes a white roux so it stays pale and milky; a blond roux belongs to velouté, a brown one to espagnole, and yolk to hollandaise.

questions.q: For a medium béchamel from 1 litre (about 1 quart) of milk, how much butter and flour do you need?
questions.why: Equal weights of butter and flour, about 60 g each to the litre, give a sauce that coats a spoon; less pours thin and more binds.

questions.q: Once a béchamel has thickened, how long should it simmer gently?
distractors: 2 to 3 minutes, as for the roux
questions.why: Flour needs time at a simmer to lose its raw, pasty taste; a béchamel that tastes of flour was rushed, not ruined.

questions.q: Which habit gives a smooth béchamel with no lumps?
questions.answer: Adding warm milk to the hot roux in stages
distractors: Pouring boiling milk onto a sizzling roux at once
Adding the flour to the hot milk last
Whisking only once the sauce has boiled
questions.why: Small additions, each whisked smooth, let the starch spread before it swells; liquid poured in all at once traps dry pockets of flour.

questions.q: In a classical béchamel, what is an onion piqué?

distractors: Onion sliced and browned in butter

questions.q: How do you keep a skin from forming on béchamel held for service?

Stir in cold water every few minutes
Turn the heat up to a rolling boil
questions.why: The skin forms where the surface meets the air; covering it, or dotting it with butter, keeps the sauce smooth to the top.

entries.title: Velouté
entries.summary: Velouté is white stock, veal, chicken or fish, thickened with a blond roux and simmered until glossy. The name means velvety. It is a working base, seldom served plain, and the root of the pale stock sauces.
entries.guest: Velouté is a silky sauce made from a light stock, chicken, veal or fish, gently thickened. It tastes savoury and mild, and lets delicate fish or chicken taste of itself.

paras: Velouté is white stock thickened with a blond roux, flour cooked in butter until it turns the colour of pale straw. White stock is made from bones that have not been roasted, so it is light in colour and clean in taste: veal, chicken or fish. The French word means velvety, and that is the aim: a sauce that is smooth, glossy and just thick enough to coat a spoon.

Where béchamel is built on milk and tastes milky, velouté is built on stock and tastes savoury. The stock is the sauce: a rich, gelatinous stock makes a velouté that needs almost nothing else, and a thin one cannot be rescued by the roux.

For 1 litre (about 1 quart) of white stock, a coating velouté takes about 60 g (2 oz) each of butter and flour. Use less for a thinner sauce or a soup base. Over a long simmer the sauce reduces and thickens, so start a little thin and let the pan do the work.

Melt the butter, add the flour and cook over a low to moderate heat for 3 to 5 minutes, stirring, until the roux is pale gold and smells nutty. Let it cool for a minute, then whisk in the hot stock a ladle at a time, whisking each addition smooth before the next. Bring it to the boil, still whisking, then lower it to a gentle simmer.

Simmer for at least 30 minutes; the old kitchens went to an hour or more. Set the pan a little off centre on the burner, so the bubbles rise on one side and push fat and scum to the other, where you lift it off with a ladle. The French call this dépouiller, to skin, and it is what turns a cloudy sauce into a clean, glossy one. Strain through a fine sieve, season late, because the sauce concentrates as it reduces, and protect the surface from a skin.

There are three veloutés, named by their stock: veal velouté, the ordinary one; chicken velouté, velouté de volaille; and fish velouté, velouté de poisson, made with fish stock. Each is the root of its own daughters, taught in the velouté family entry. A velouté is rarely served plain: it is a working base, finished at the last moment with cream, egg yolks, wine or butter for the plate in front of it.

The same idea makes a velouté soup: a velouté base, often with a purée of the main ingredient, thinned with stock, then finished off the boil with a liaison, egg yolk and cream whisked in to enrich and thicken it. On modern menus the word also names almost any silky puréed soup.

A greasy surface means poor skimming: the fat that rose during the simmer was stirred back in instead of lifted off. Skim it now, off centre, and strain. A grey or dull beige cast comes from a roux taken past blond, or from hard whisking in an aluminium pan; cook the roux only to pale gold and use stainless steel. A thin body comes from weak stock. Reduce it longer if the taste is there, but a watery stock makes a watery sauce. Lumps and a raw flour taste have the same causes and cures as in béchamel.

A server meets velouté mostly in its daughters, which carry names of their own. Describe it as a silky sauce of light stock, chicken, veal or fish, gently thickened. It is savoury, not milky. Any question about what goes into it, the stock, the flour or the cream, goes to the kitchen.

questions.q: How is a velouté soup finished, once the base is thinned with stock?
questions.answer: Off the boil, with yolk and cream
distractors: With a brown roux whisked in hard
At a rolling boil, with more flour
With cold butter and a splash of vinegar

questions.q: How is velouté most often used in a classical kitchen?
questions.answer: As a base for small sauces
distractors: Served plain as a dipping sauce
As a thickener for brown stock

entries.title: Espagnole
entries.summary: Espagnole is brown stock thickened with a brown roux, built with browned mirepoix, tomato and often bacon, then simmered for hours and skimmed. Rarely served alone, it is the parent of demi-glace and so of the whole brown family.
entries.guest: Espagnole is the classic French brown sauce: roasted stock, browned vegetables and tomato, slowly simmered. It is the base behind demi-glace and the dark, meaty steak sauces.

paras: Espagnole is the brown mother sauce: brown stock, made from roasted bones, thickened with a brown roux. It is built with a mirepoix, diced onion and carrot and often celery, browned in fat, with tomato and often a little bacon or ham. It simmers for hours while the cook skims it, until it is deep brown, glossy and full of roasted, meaty flavour.

It is rarely served alone. Its job is to become demi-glace, espagnole and brown stock reduced together, and from demi-glace come the brown sauces of the classical kitchen. Learn espagnole and you know where a steak sauce's depth comes from.

A working ratio is 80 to 100 g (about 3 oz) of brown roux, equal weights of fat and flour, to 1 litre (about 1 quart) of brown stock. A brown roux thickens less than a pale one, because the long cooking breaks down some of the starch, so espagnole takes more roux than a velouté. Add about 150 g (5 oz) of mirepoix and a spoonful or two of tomato purée, and expect the long simmer to reduce the sauce by a third or more.

Brown the mirepoix, with diced bacon or ham if you use it, in fat over a moderate heat until well coloured but never burnt. Add the flour, or a brown roux made separately, and cook it, stirring, for 8 to 15 minutes until it reaches the colour of milky coffee or hazelnut and smells of toasted nuts.

Add the hot brown stock in stages, whisking each addition smooth. Stir in the tomato and a bouquet garni, a bundle of thyme, bay and parsley stalks tied together, bring it to the boil, then lower it to a lazy simmer. Simmer for several hours, two to three at the least, with the pan set off centre so the fat and scum gather on one side, and skim them away steadily. Top up with stock if it reduces too fast. Strain through a fine sieve, pressing lightly, and cool it quickly if it is not used at once.

Bitterness comes from a roux taken too dark, or from bones and vegetables scorched in the roasting. It cannot be skimmed or strained out, so judge the roux before the stock goes in. A gluey, pasty sauce has too much roux for its stock, or has been reduced too far; loosen it with stock. A greasy sauce has not been skimmed enough, so skim off centre and strain. A raw, floury taste means it was rushed: give it more time. Season only at the end, because hours of reduction concentrate any salt in the stock.

Espagnole means Spanish, and nobody knows for certain why. Stories credit Spanish cooks at the French court, Spanish ham or Spanish tomatoes; tell any of them as tradition, not fact. The sauce held its place at the head of the brown sauces from Carême's four through Escoffier's base sauces.

Many modern kitchens skip it. They roast more bones, make a stronger brown stock and simply reduce it, sometimes binding it lightly with arrowroot or cornflour, to a jus or a flourless demi-glace. They gain a cleaner, brighter taste, a glossier sauce, no flour to cook out and less time at the stove. They lose the economy of a sauce that stretched its stock with roux, the rounded depth of the long simmer with tomato and mirepoix, and a body that does not rest on gelatin alone. Which road a kitchen takes is its chef's call.

A guest rarely sees the word espagnole on a menu; they meet it inside a brown sauce. Describe it as the classic French brown sauce, slow-cooked from roasted stock, browned vegetables and tomato. If a guest asks whether a brown sauce is thickened with flour, that question goes to the kitchen, because kitchens build their brown sauces in different ways.

entries.title: Sauce tomate
entries.summary: The classical French tomato sauce: tomatoes cooked with salt pork, a mirepoix, garlic and white stock, then passed through a sieve until smooth. One of Escoffier's four base sauces, it is the parent of provençale and portugaise, and New Orleans' Creole sauce is its cousin.
entries.guest: Sauce tomate is the French kitchen's tomato sauce: ripe tomatoes slow cooked with a little pork, vegetables and stock, then sieved smooth. It is rounder and silkier than a quick tomato sauce.

paras: Sauce tomate is the French kitchen's tomato sauce, and one of the five mother sauces taught today. Tomatoes are cooked slowly with salt pork or bacon, a mirepoix (diced carrot and onion cooked in fat as a flavour base), garlic, herbs and white stock, then sieved so only a smooth, brick red sauce comes through. Most kitchens now thicken it by reduction alone, cooking it down until it coats a spoon, rather than with a roux.
It matters because so much grows from it, and in New Orleans its nearest cousin is the Creole sauce.

Render 50 g (2 oz) of diced salt pork or unsmoked bacon in a little butter over gentle heat until the fat runs. Add 75 g (2.5 oz) each of diced carrot and onion, a bay leaf and a sprig of thyme, and cook for 8 to 10 minutes until soft and lightly golden. For the classical version, stir in 30 g (1 oz) of flour and cook it for 2 minutes.

Add 2 kg (4.4 lb) of ripe tomatoes, roughly chopped, or the same weight of tinned plum tomatoes with their juice, then 500 ml (about 2 cups) of white stock, a crushed clove of garlic, salt, pepper and a pinch of sugar. Bring it to the boil, cover and cook in a low oven, about 160°C (320°F), or at the barest simmer on the stove, for 1.5 to 2 hours, stirring from the bottom now and then.

Pass it through a food mill or fine sieve, pressing the pulp through and leaving skins, seeds, pork and vegetables behind. Reduce it gently in a clean pan until it coats a spoon, taste for salt and acidity, and dot the surface with butter so no skin forms. It makes a little over 1 litre (about 1 quart).

The daughters are made by addition. Provençale brings garlic and olive oil, with parsley or other herbs. Portugaise softens chopped onion in oil, then adds garlic, chopped tomato flesh and parsley. In New Orleans the family has a cousin in the Creole sauce, built on the holy trinity of onion, celery and green pepper, with a logic of its own rather than a classical daughter's; at Brennan's it is the sauce on the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits.

An Italian sugo is a cousin, not a daughter: usually tomatoes, olive oil, garlic or onion and perhaps basil, cooked for a shorter time and often left with some texture. Sauce tomate has stock, pork and mirepoix behind it, cooks longer and is sieved smooth, so it tastes rounder and meatier.

Raw acidity, a sharp, thin taste, comes from underripe tomatoes or too short a cook: cook it longer and round it with a pinch of sugar or a piece of butter. A scorched base comes from tomato sugars catching on the pan: use a heavy pan and gentle heat, stir from the bottom, and if it catches, pour the sauce into a clean pan without scraping and taste it; a burnt note that runs through means starting again. A sauce too thin to coat needs more gentle reduction after sieving, never a spoonful of raw flour.

Carême's four great sauces, in the early nineteenth century, had no tomato among them; Escoffier counted sauce tomate among his four base sauces in Le Guide culinaire (1903). He fried diced salt pork with carrot and onion, stirred in a little flour as a light roux, added tomatoes, white stock and garlic, and cooked it covered in the oven before sieving it. Later cooks dropped the flour and let reduction do the work, for a brighter sauce.

Choose for ripeness. In their summer season, ripe Creole tomatoes, Louisiana's own, make a sweet, bright sauce. The rest of the year, good tinned plum tomatoes, picked and packed ripe, beat pale fresh ones; plum varieties carry more flesh and less water, so they cook down faster.

At the table, call it a smooth, slow-cooked tomato sauce, rounder than a quick marinara because it is cooked with stock and a little pork. Mention both to a guest who avoids pork or meat, and send every such question to the kitchen, because a house recipe may differ from the classical one.

entries.title: Hollandaise
entries.summary: A warm emulsion of egg yolk and butter, sharpened with lemon juice or a vinegar reduction. It is the one mother sauce bound by egg yolk: quick to make, fragile in service and the parent of a whole family.
entries.guest: Hollandaise is a warm butter sauce thickened with egg yolk and brightened with lemon. On the Eggs Hussarde it shares the plate with a red wine sauce.

paras: Hollandaise is a warm emulsion: tiny droplets of butterfat held apart in a little water by egg yolk, whose proteins and lecithin, a natural emulsifier, coat each droplet so it cannot join the next. Acid, either lemon juice or a reduction of vinegar and peppercorns, sharpens the flavour and helps the yolk stay smooth under heat. It is the one mother sauce thickened by yolk rather than by roux or reduction, which makes it quick, fragile and unforgiving of carelessness.
For a new cook it is the sauce that teaches heat control; for a server, the sauce guests know from Eggs Benedict and the door into a large family, béarnaise first.

Allow about one yolk for every 60 to 85 g (2 to 3 oz) of butter. A dependable batch is 3 yolks to 225 g (8 oz) of clarified butter, about 75 g a yolk, with 30 ml (2 tbsp) of reduction or lemon juice, a spoonful of water, salt and a pinch of cayenne. One yolk can hold far more fat, but a sauce pushed to its limit breaks at the first knock, so the ratio buys a margin for service.
Clarified butter, with its water and milk solids removed, gives a firmer, steadier hollandaise; whole melted butter brings its own water and gives a lighter, looser sauce with a milkier taste.

Reduce white wine vinegar with crushed white peppercorns and a little water, strain it and let it cool. Whisk the yolks with the reduction in a bowl set over barely simmering water, never touching it, until they foam and then thicken into a pale ribbon that holds its shape for a moment. That happens at about 60 to 65°C (140 to 149°F). Past about 70°C (158°F) the yolk proteins begin to set into curds, so lift the bowl away whenever the edges thicken too fast.

Off the heat, whisk in the warm butter a few drops at a time until the sauce takes, then in a thin, steady stream. Season with salt, a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of cayenne. If it stiffens, loosen it with a few drops of warm water.

Read the finished sauce by eye and spoon. It should coat the spoon thickly enough to hold a line drawn through it with a finger, look glossy rather than dull or oily, be pale yellow, and feel warm, never hot: around 60°C (140°F). Keeping it there through a long service is its own lesson, in the entry on holding warm emulsions.

A hollandaise fails in two directions. Too hot, and the yolk scrambles into a grainy, curdled sauce. Butter added too fast, a base gone too cool, or a sauce pushed too thick with too little water, and the fat escapes, leaving a greasy, split pool. The quick fix for a split is to whisk the broken sauce, drop by drop, into a spoonful of warm water or a fresh yolk in a clean bowl. The full set of rescues belongs to the entry on breaking and rescuing.

The name means Dutch sauce, though no clear link to Holland has been found. Modern kitchens teach hollandaise as the fifth mother sauce. Carême's four great sauces did not include it, and Escoffier's French Le Guide culinaire (1903) named four base sauces and placed hollandaise among the smaller sauces. The English translation of 1907, A Guide to Modern Cookery, prints it in its chapter of leading warm sauces, and later schools made five the standard lesson. It earns its place as a mother through its large family.

On the floor, describe hollandaise as a warm butter sauce thickened with egg yolk and brightened with lemon, the sauce guests know from Eggs Benedict. Its yolks are only lightly cooked, so any question about eggs, butter or how the sauce is made goes to the kitchen, never to a guess.

At Brennan's, hollandaise is the rich, lemony layer on the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen. Each pairs it with marchand de vin, a dark red wine sauce beneath the egg, so the plate carries one bright sauce and one deep one. Describe it as the classic Benedict sauce, and send any question about what goes into it to the kitchen.

entries.title: Béarnaise
entries.summary: Hollandaise built on a sharp reduction of white wine, tarragon vinegar, shallot and tarragon, and finished with fresh herbs. Firmer and sharper than its parent, it is the classic sauce for grilled beef and the base of Choron and Foyot.
entries.guest: Béarnaise is a warm butter and egg yolk sauce sharpened with tarragon and shallot. It is the classic French sauce for steak, and it comes with our breakfast hanger steak.

paras: Béarnaise is hollandaise's best-known daughter: a warm emulsion of egg yolk and butter, built on its own sharp reduction. White wine, tarragon vinegar, chopped shallot, tarragon stalks, chervil and crushed peppercorns are boiled down until almost dry, and that concentrate flavours the whole sauce. Tarragon is a herb with a clear aniseed note; chervil is a soft herb, milder and sweeter. Both go in again, fresh and chopped, at the end.
The acid and the herbs give béarnaise a sharper, greener taste and a firmer body than hollandaise, which is why it stands up to grilled and roast beef.

For 3 yolks and 225 g (8 oz) of clarified or melted butter, put 60 ml (1/4 cup) of tarragon or white wine vinegar and 60 ml (1/4 cup) of dry white wine in a small pan with two finely chopped shallots, a few tarragon stalks, a sprig of chervil and a pinch of crushed peppercorns. Reduce until only about 30 ml (2 tbsp) of liquid is left, almost dry. The reduction should taste fiercely sharp on its own, because the butter will soften it a great deal.

Let the reduction cool a little, then strain it for a smooth sauce, or leave the shallot in for texture; both are seen in good kitchens. Whisk it with the yolks over barely simmering water until they thicken to a ribbon, at about 60 to 65°C (140 to 149°F), then take the bowl off the heat and mount the warm butter in, slowly at first. To mount is to whisk fat into a sauce so that it thickens and shines.
Béarnaise is usually made a little thicker than hollandaise, so it sits on hot meat instead of running off it. Finish with chopped tarragon and chervil, taste for salt, and keep it warm, never hot.
Béarnaise breaks for the same reasons as hollandaise, overheated yolks or butter added too fast, and it mends the same way: whisk it drop by drop into a little warm water or a fresh yolk.

Three faults are its own. A reduction left too wet carries too much water into the yolks, and the sauce comes out thin and slack; next time boil it down further, and for now whisk the thin sauce into a fresh yolk over gentle heat. A reduction too heavy on vinegar makes the sauce harsh; soften it with a little more butter. A sauce that tastes flat had a timid reduction: a few drops of vinegar and more fresh tarragon bring it back. Dried tarragon cannot stand in at the finish.

Tradition credits the sauce to the chef Collinet at the Pavillon Henri IV in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, around 1836, and says he named it for Béarn, the region of south-west France where Henri IV was born. The date and even the chef's name vary between accounts, so tell it as tradition. Its place in the classical repertoire is not in doubt: it is the best-known daughter of hollandaise.

Béarnaise has children of its own. Choron folds in tomato cooked down to a paste, which turns the sauce a soft coral without thinning it. Foyot, which many texts also call Valois, whisks in glace de viande, a reduced meat glaze, for a tawny, deeper sauce. Foyot keeps the fresh tarragon; Escoffier's Choron leaves out the final chopped tarragon and chervil, though many kitchens keep them. Both have their own entry.

At Brennan's, béarnaise is printed on the breakfast Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak as French béarnaise, beside a sunny-side-up egg and a smoked potato pavé, a neat, layered block of potato. Its daughters work elsewhere on the menu: Choron replaces the usual hollandaise on the Eggs Sardou, and Foyot brings depth to the Roasted Chateaubriand, a lean cut given a rich sauce.

To a guest, béarnaise is a warm butter and egg yolk sauce sharpened with shallot and tarragon, the classic French sauce for steak. A guest who knows hollandaise can hear it as hollandaise's sharper, herbal daughter. Any question about eggs, butter or how it is made goes to the kitchen.

entries.title: Marchand de vin
entries.summary: The wine merchant's sauce: red wine and shallot reduced into a brown sauce. New Orleans made its own glossy version of onion, garlic, often ham and mushroom, red wine and beef stock, and Brennan's serves it beneath the egg on the Eggs Hussarde.
entries.guest: Marchand de vin, the wine merchant's sauce, is a savoury, glossy red wine sauce, often with mushroom. On the Eggs Hussarde it sits beneath the egg, with hollandaise on top.

paras: Marchand de vin means wine merchant, and the sauce is named for what he sold: red wine, reduced with shallots and finished as a brown sauce. In France it is shallots cooked down in red wine with demi-glace (brown stock and brown sauce reduced until glossy), or a butter beaten with the same flavours and melted over a grilled steak. Either way it tastes of wine first and meat second.

New Orleans made its own version, and it is the one a Brennan's server needs. Onion and plenty of garlic stand in for some or all of the shallot, ham and mushrooms often join them, and red wine and beef stock are frequently bound with a roux into a glossy brown sauce, thicker and more savoury than the French reduction.

For the New Orleans style, melt 45 g (1.5 oz) of butter and cook a small onion, finely chopped, four cloves of garlic, 60 g (2 oz) of diced ham and 115 g (4 oz) of sliced mushrooms over moderate heat for 8 to 10 minutes, until soft and lightly browned. Stir in 30 g (1 oz) of flour and keep stirring for 5 to 8 minutes, until it smells nutty and turns light brown. That is a roux, flour cooked in fat, and it will thicken the sauce.

Pour in 250 ml (about 1 cup) of red wine and boil it down by half, which drives off the raw alcohol and concentrates the fruit. Add 500 ml (about 2 cups) of beef stock, a bay leaf and a sprig of thyme, and simmer gently for 20 to 30 minutes, skimming off any fat, until the sauce coats the back of a spoon. Season with salt, black pepper and a pinch of cayenne, and lift out the herbs.

The French sauce is quicker: reduce two finely chopped shallots in 250 ml (about 1 cup) of red wine by two thirds, add 250 ml (about 1 cup) of demi-glace, simmer for a few minutes, and finish off the heat with a knob of cold butter.

In the sauce tree, marchand de vin is a daughter of the brown family: a brown base, an aromatic and an acid reduction, here red wine. Its closest cousin is bordelaise, the French red wine sauce finished with beef marrow; bordelaise has its own entry, and in New Orleans its own meaning.

A raw, sharp taste of wine means the wine went in with the stock before it was reduced; reduce it by half first. A floury, pasty taste means the roux was not cooked long enough, or the sauce was not simmered after thickening; simmer it longer. A gluey, heavy sauce has too much roux or too much reduction; loosen it with hot stock. A greasy surface is fat from the ham and butter left in; draw the pan half off the heat so the fat gathers on one side, and skim it. A bitter sauce has burnt garlic or a scorched roux, which nothing hides: start again.

Classical French cooking used the wine merchant's flavours both as a sauce and as a butter for grilled steak. In New Orleans, Antoine's, open since 1840, is credited with making the sauce famous in the city. Eggs Hussarde, which Brennan's made famous from about 1950, put the sauce on the breakfast table, under poached eggs and beside hollandaise.

At the table, call it a savoury red wine and mushroom sauce, the house wording, once lineup has confirmed that tonight's carries mushroom; until then, a savoury red wine sauce. Never call it a bare red wine reduction, which undersells a sauce with real body. Whether it carries ham tonight, or what thickens it, is the chef's answer, not a guess. It is made with red wine, which matters to a guest who avoids alcohol; the kitchen confirms the rest.

At Brennan's, marchand de vin is the dark, winey half of the two sauces on the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen, beneath the egg with hollandaise above; on the Owen it echoes the short rib braised in red wine. New Orleans marchand de vin is often bound with a roux; whether ours is, and how dark that roux goes, is a question for the chef.

entries.title: Choron and Foyot
entries.summary: Two daughters of béarnaise, each made by one addition. Choron folds in tomato cooked down to a thick paste, coral and tangy; Foyot whisks in glace de viande, a reduced meat glaze, tawny and deeper. Brennan's serves both.
entries.guest: Both are béarnaise, the warm tarragon butter sauce. Choron adds tomato, tangy and herbal, on our Eggs Sardou; Foyot adds a reduced beef glaze, richer, with the Chateaubriand.

paras: Choron and Foyot are two daughters of béarnaise, the warm emulsion of egg yolk and butter built on a sharp reduction of vinegar, shallot and tarragon. An emulsion is fat held as tiny droplets in a little water, here by the yolk. Each daughter is one addition to a finished béarnaise. Choron folds in tomato cooked down to a thick paste, which turns the sauce coral, a soft orange pink, and adds a gentle sweetness and tang under the herbs.

Foyot whisks in glace de viande, brown stock boiled down until thick and syrupy, which turns the sauce tawny and gives it a deep, savoury, meaty taste. Both are on the Brennan's menu: learn the parent, then the one addition.

Start from a sound béarnaise: about 3 yolks to 225 g (8 oz) of butter gives roughly 300 ml (1 1/4 cups) of sauce. For Choron, fold in 2 to 3 tbsp (30 to 45 ml) of tomato reduced to a paste, about one part to six of sauce. For Foyot, whisk in 1 to 2 tbsp (15 to 30 ml) of warm, melted glace de viande, a spoonful at a time, because glace is strong and often salty; season only at the end.

Make the tomato first. Cook chopped ripe tomatoes, or good tinned purée, in a wide pan over moderate heat, stirring often, until the water has gone and a spoon drawn through leaves a clear line; pass it through a fine sieve and let it cool to warm. Tomato paste cooked for a minute in a dry pan does the same job. Make the béarnaise, then fold the warm tomato through it off the heat. Escoffier's Choron leaves out the final chopped tarragon and chervil; many kitchens keep them.

For Foyot, melt the glace without boiling it and whisk it into the finished béarnaise a spoonful at a time, tasting as you go. Hold both like béarnaise: warm, around 60°C (140°F), in a bain-marie, a pan of warm water, never on direct heat, and made in small batches through service.

Wet tomato is the classic fault, and the reason the tomato is reduced. Fresh tomato is mostly water, and a sauce of yolk and butter has little water to spare: watery purée makes Choron thin and slack, and if the balance tips far enough it splits into a greasy pool. Tomato cold from the fridge can break it too, and raw tomato leaves a sharp, metallic edge that cooking down softens.

Foyot fails differently: too much glace makes it salty, heavy and muddy, and cold glace sets in streaks before it blends. A split sauce of either kind is mended like any béarnaise, whisked drop by drop into a little warm water or a fresh yolk in a clean bowl.

Choron is named for Alexandre Étienne Choron, chef de cuisine at the Voisin restaurant in Paris, remembered for the Christmas menu he served there in 1870, during the Siege of Paris, when the cut-off city ate whatever it could find. Whether he created the sauce or it was named in his honour is not recorded, so tell it as tradition.

Foyot takes its name from the Restaurant Foyot in Paris, on the rue de Tournon facing the Senate. Many texts call the same sauce Valois; others treat the two as separate sauces and disagree on what divides them, so teach both names.

At Brennan's, Choron replaces the usual hollandaise on the Eggs Sardou, over poached eggs, crispy artichokes and Parmesan creamed spinach; the house words for it are tangy and herbal. Foyot comes with the Roasted Chateaubriand, the centre of the beef tenderloin roasted whole for two. Tenderloin is lean and mild, so a rich, savoury sauce brings the depth the meat lacks.

Say sho-ROHN and fwah-YO, the weight on the last syllable of each. To a guest, Choron is béarnaise with tomato, tangy and herbal; Foyot is béarnaise made richer with a reduced beef glaze. Both are made with egg yolk and butter, so any question about eggs or dairy goes to the service note and the kitchen.

entries.title: Demi-glace
entries.summary: Espagnole and brown stock simmered together and reduced by half until glossy: the working mother of the classical brown sauces. Bordelaise, Robert, chasseur, madère and périgueux start from it, and many modern kitchens make it from reduced brown stock alone.
entries.guest: Demi-glace is a deep, glossy brown sauce made by slowly reducing roasted veal or beef stock. It is the base of the classic French steak sauces.

paras: Demi-glace means half glaze: a brown sauce reduced halfway towards glace, the thick, syrupy glaze that sets hard when cold. Classically it is espagnole, the roux-thickened brown sauce, simmered with an equal amount of brown stock and reduced by half, then skimmed, strained and often finished with Madeira or dry sherry. Brown stock is made from roasted bones and vegetables, so demi-glace tastes of roasting: deep, meaty and rounded, with body from the roux and from the gelatin of the bones.

It matters because it is the working mother of the brown family. Espagnole is rarely served as it is; demi-glace is what the saucier, the cook in charge of sauces, reaches for to start a bordelaise, a Robert or a chasseur.

Classical demi-glace is equal parts espagnole and brown stock, reduced by half: 1 litre (about 1 quart) of each, simmered down to about 1 litre (about 1 quart), then finished off the heat with about 100 ml (about 7 tbsp) of Madeira or dry sherry. For the modern version, roughly 4 litres (about 1 gallon) of brown stock reduces to 1 litre (about 1 quart).

Bring the espagnole and stock to a simmer in a heavy pan set slightly off centre on the heat, so the liquid rolls up on one side only. Fat and scum gather on the quiet side, where they are skimmed away: the French call this dépouiller. Reduce slowly, skimming every 10 to 15 minutes, until it has lost about half its volume and coats a spoon, two to three hours for a large batch. Pass it through a chinois, a fine conical sieve, lined with muslin for the finest result. Add the wine off the heat, because boiling drives off its perfume.

Many modern kitchens skip espagnole and reduce good brown stock alone the same way. Without roux it is lighter and clearer, its body all gelatin, though it costs more bones and turns sticky if pushed too far. The cues are the same: glossy, nappe (coating a spoon so a finger leaves a clean line), a clean meaty taste, no raw flour, no beads of fat. Cool it from 57°C (135°F) to 21°C (70°F) within two hours and to 5°C (41°F) within six hours in all, as the FDA Food Code sets out.

Demi-glace is the parent the brown daughters share. Bordelaise adds a red wine and shallot reduction and beef marrow; Robert, onion, white wine and mustard; chasseur, the hunter's sauce, mushrooms, shallot, white wine, tomato and tarragon. Madère is demi-glace finished with Madeira, and périgueux adds truffle to madère. The pattern is an aromatic, an acid reduction, the demi-glace and a finish. Reduced further still, brown stock becomes glace de viande.

A gluey, pasty demi-glace had too much roux or was reduced too far: loosen it with brown stock. Bitterness comes from scorching, bones roasted black or a sauce caught on the pan, and cannot be taken out, so the batch is remade. Saltiness comes from salted stock, because reduction concentrates every grain; stock meant for demi-glace is never salted. A greasy surface means poor skimming, and a dull, cloudy sauce was boiled hard.

Bought bases run from frozen, kitchen-quality demi-glace to powders and pastes, and a professional kitchen judges them on the label and in the pan. Stock, or bones and vegetables, should come first, not salt, starch or sugar. Reconstitute it and taste it plain beside the house stock: it should taste of roasted meat, not salt or caramel colouring, and set to a jelly when chilled, the sign of real gelatin. Starch-thickened bases turn pasty when reduced, so test one in a pan sauce before it reaches the line.

Guests rarely meet demi-glace by name; they meet its daughters. Describe it plainly: a deep, glossy brown sauce made by slowly reducing roasted veal or beef stock, the base of the classic French steak sauces. At Brennan's the brown side of the tree shows in the marchand de vin on the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen; how the kitchen builds that sauce is a question for the chef before you describe it.

entries.title: Bordelaise, French and New Orleans
entries.summary: Two sauces share the name. French bordelaise is red wine, shallot and herbs reduced into demi-glace and finished with beef marrow; New Orleans bordelaise is a garlic butter with parsley. Knowing which is on the plate changes the wine and the promise.
entries.guest: Here bordelaise can mean two sauces: the French red wine sauce for steak, or the New Orleans garlic and parsley butter. I'll confirm which is on your plate tonight.

paras: Bordelaise, in the Bordeaux style, names two different sauces. French bordelaise is a brown sauce: red wine reduced with shallot, thyme, bay and pepper, simmered with demi-glace, strained, and finished with poached diced beef marrow and parsley. Marrow is the soft fat inside a beef leg bone; poached gently, it melts on the tongue. The sauce is dark, glossy and winey, the steakhouse classic with a porterhouse or an entrecôte, a rib steak.

New Orleans bordelaise is something else: butter, often with olive oil, warmed with plenty of garlic and parsley, sometimes shallot or green onion, and spooned over fish, oysters, pasta or bread. It is pale, fragrant and buttery, with no red wine at all.

For about 500 ml (2 cups) of French bordelaise: 250 ml (1 cup) of red wine with 2 chopped shallots, a sprig of thyme, half a bay leaf and crushed pepper, reduced by three quarters; then 500 ml (2 cups) of demi-glace; then about 100 g (3 1/2 oz) of diced marrow. For New Orleans bordelaise, use 225 g (8 oz) of butter, or butter and olive oil, to 4 to 6 cloves of garlic and a handful of chopped parsley.

French method. Sweat the shallot in a little butter, add the wine, thyme, bay and pepper, and boil until a quarter is left; reduced wine tastes rounder and less sharp. Add the demi-glace and simmer gently, skimming, for 20 to 30 minutes, until it coats a spoon, then strain it through a chinois. Soak the marrow in cold water, dice it and poach it for a minute or two in salted water just below a simmer; boiling would melt it away. Add it at the last moment with the parsley, and a piece of cold butter for gloss.

New Orleans method. Warm the butter and oil over low heat, add finely chopped garlic and cook it gently until soft and fragrant but not brown, then add parsley, salt and pepper; some cooks add lemon or a splash of white wine. Make it close to service, because garlic and parsley fade when held.

The name is for Bordeaux and its red wine. Escoffier's Guide gives bordelaise with red wine, the standard today; a white wine bordelaise is said to be the older, and Escoffier also recorded a white wine version under the name Bonnefoy. Bordeaux cooking uses à la bordelaise for other dishes too: cèpes à la bordelaise are mushrooms sautéed in oil with shallot, parsley and often garlic. How New Orleans came to use the word for a garlic butter is not settled, so give no origin story at the table.

French bordelaise turns thin and sour when the wine is not reduced enough before the demi-glace goes in. Boiled marrow melts into grease; poach it gently and add it last. A gluey sauce had a heavy demi-glace, and brown stock loosens it. New Orleans bordelaise turns bitter and acrid when the garlic browns, so start it in barely warm fat. Held too long, the parsley turns khaki and the garlic flat.

On the Brennan's breakfast and lunch menu, the Pecan Gulf Fish, today's Gulf fish topped with lump crab over cauliflower purée and collard greens, carries a pecan bordelaise. The house reading is that it most likely belongs to the New Orleans family, a butter sauce with toasted pecans worked in. That is a reading, not a recipe: confirm at lineup whether tonight's is garlic butter or red wine based, because it decides the wine. The house pour is the Gainey Chardonnay; if the sauce is red wine based, the Damien Martin Bourgogne Pinot Noir takes its place.

The difference matters at the table: a red wine and marrow sauce wants a red with some structure, and a garlic butter on fish wants a white. Never promise red wine or marrow until the kitchen confirms which bordelaise it is. To a guest: French bordelaise is a rich red wine sauce for steak; New Orleans bordelaise is a garlic and parsley butter. Questions about what is in the sauce go to the kitchen.

entries.title: The béchamel family
entries.summary: The small sauces built on béchamel: Mornay with cheese, Soubise with onion, Nantua with crayfish, crème with cream and cardinal with lobster butter. Each is béchamel plus one defining addition, and the cousins run from macaroni cheese to Oysters Bienville.
entries.guest: These are creamy white sauces built on béchamel, milk thickened with butter and flour. Mornay adds cheese, Soubise sweet onion and Nantua crayfish, classics for gratins and fish.

paras: The béchamel family is every sauce made by adding one thing to béchamel, the white sauce of milk thickened with a white roux, flour cooked in butter without colour. Béchamel is mild by design, which is why it takes additions so well: cheese, onion, cream, a crayfish or lobster butter. Learn the addition and the name tells you the sauce's colour, its taste and what it goes with.

Mornay is béchamel with grated Gruyère and Parmesan melted in off the heat, finished with a little butter and sometimes an egg yolk, which helps it set and brown. It is the sauce of gratins and of glazing, browning a sauce under a hot grill; for fish, classical kitchens add some fish fumet, a concentrated fish stock. Soubise is béchamel with a purée of onions cooked slowly in butter until soft and sweet but never coloured. The older Soubise was onion cooked with rice and puréed; both are ivory, mild and sweet.

Nantua is béchamel with cream and crayfish butter, butter pounded with crayfish shells and strained, garnished with crayfish tails: pink and rich, named for Nantua, a town in the Ain known for its crayfish. It is the classic sauce for quenelles de brochet, poached dumplings of pike, a dish of Lyon. Crème is béchamel reduced with cream and finished with more cream and lemon. Cardinal is béchamel with fish fumet, finished with lobster butter and a pinch of cayenne: coral red.

Make a medium béchamel and cook it out for at least 15 to 20 minutes so no taste of raw flour remains. For Mornay, take the pan off the heat before the cheese goes in, because boiled cheese turns stringy and oily; stir it in a handful at a time, then the butter. For Soubise, sweat sliced onions in butter under a lid, with a splash of water if they threaten to colour, until completely soft, 30 to 40 minutes, then stir them into the béchamel and blend it smooth. For Nantua and cardinal, reduce the béchamel with cream or fumet, then whisk in the crayfish or lobster butter off the heat.

For Mornay, a common working ratio is 1 litre (about 1 quart) of medium béchamel to 100 to 125 g (about 4 oz) of grated cheese, half Gruyère and half Parmesan, and 50 g (2 oz) of butter. For Soubise, about 500 g (1 lb) of onions to 500 ml (2 cups) of béchamel. For crème, reduce 1 litre (about 1 quart) of béchamel with 250 ml (1 cup) of cream, then finish with more cream and lemon.

A grainy or stringy Mornay was boiled after the cheese went in, or made with pre-grated cheese coated in starch: grate it fresh and add it off the heat. An oily Mornay had too much cheese or heat; whisk in a little hot milk. A beige Soubise had its onions coloured, and the only fix is to start them again, low and covered. A gratin that will not brown needs a yolk or more cheese in the sauce and a hotter grill. A Nantua or cardinal that separates had its crayfish or lobster butter added too hot: whisk in a spoonful of hot cream off the heat.

The cheese sauce of the American kitchen, Cheddar melted into béchamel for macaroni cheese, is Mornay's later cousin, and so is the bistro's mustard sauce, béchamel sharpened with Dijon for ham or fish. The croque-monsieur, a toasted ham and Gruyère sandwich, is the everyday Mornay: many cafés top it with Mornay or béchamel and grill it until bubbling, and the croque-madame adds a fried egg.

New Orleans has its own cousin in the sauce of Oysters Bienville: a rich cream sauce with shrimp, mushroom and sherry, baked over oysters on the half shell and gratinéed, browned under heat with a crust of breadcrumbs or cheese.

To a guest, each is a creamy white sauce, and the addition describes it: Mornay is a cheese sauce, Soubise a sweet onion cream, Nantua a crayfish cream. A dish au gratin or Mornay has a browned cheese crust over a creamy sauce. Any question about dairy, gluten or shellfish in these sauces goes to the service note and the kitchen.

entries.title: The velouté family
entries.summary: The daughters of velouté: suprême and allemande on the chicken and veal side, vin blanc, Bercy and normande on the fish side, and a run of small sauces each made by one addition. Learn the stock, then the finish.
entries.guest: A velouté sauce is a pale, silky sauce made from a light stock of chicken, veal or fish, finished with cream, egg yolk, white wine or butter.

paras: Velouté is seldom served as it is. It is a working base, and the sauces a guest meets are its daughters, each finished at the last moment with one or two things that give it a name: cream makes it rich, egg yolks thick and golden, white wine and fish stock taste of the sea, tomato turns it pink. Know the stock and the finish, and any name can be read.

The family splits along the stock: chicken and veal veloutés give suprême and allemande and most of the meat side; fish velouté, made with fumet, a concentrated fish stock, gives the white wine sauces of poached fish.

Suprême is chicken velouté reduced with cream and a little mushroom cooking liquor, then finished with butter. For 1 litre (about 1 quart) of velouté, add about 250 ml (1 cup) of cream in stages as it reduces, and stop when it is nappe, coating the back of a spoon. Off the heat, swirl in 50 g (about 2 oz) of cold butter: ivory, creamy and clean.

Allemande, which Escoffier also called sauce parisienne, is veal velouté bound with egg yolks and lemon. Whisk 4 or 5 yolks with a little cold stock and mushroom liquor, then temper them: whisk in a ladle of hot velouté so they warm gradually, and pour it all back into the pan. This egg finish is a liaison. Bring it back to a simmer, stirring, and reduce it until it coats the spoon: the flour protects the yolks, though a long, hard boil can still grain them. Finish with lemon, nutmeg and butter, and strain.

From allemande comes poulette, with more mushroom liquor, lemon and chopped parsley, the classic sauce for mussels. From suprême comes ivoire, tinted the colour of old ivory with pale chicken glaze, glace de volaille, and from ivoire comes Albuféra, finished with a red pepper butter. Aurore is velouté with tomato cooked down to a paste, pink as the dawn it is named for. Hongroise is onion and paprika softened in butter, white wine reduced over them, then velouté, simmered and strained.

On the fish side, vin blanc is fish velouté with fumet and yolks, finished with butter. Bercy starts with shallot sweated in butter, white wine and fumet reduced over it, then fish velouté, butter and parsley. Normande, the richest, adds mushroom and oyster liquor, yolks and cream. Warm ravigote is velouté with a white wine and vinegar reduction, finished with shallot butter and chopped chervil, tarragon and chives, three of the fines herbes.

Read them by eye and tongue. Suprême is ivory and creamy; allemande is deeper yellow, with a lemon edge; poulette is the same, flecked green. Aurore is coral, hongroise soft salmon and warm with paprika. The fish sauces are pale, glossy and taste of the sea; Bercy shows specks of shallot, ravigote flecks of herb.

Every fault of the velouté passes to its daughters, so mend the base first. The flour in a velouté protects a yolk liaison, so allemande and normande can be reduced with their yolks in, but a long, hard boil still grains them into specks: strain at once and whisk in a little cold cream. A liaison of yolk and cream with no flour behind it, as on a velouté soup, curdles above about 85°C (185°F), so it goes in off the boil. A cream sauce reduced too far turns heavy and oily; loosen it with hot stock. Wine added late tastes raw, so reduce it first.

Sole Véronique, poached sole in a white wine sauce with peeled muscat grapes, glazed under the grill, is the classical ancestor of the Redfish Véronique. Tradition credits it to Escoffier at the Carlton Hotel in London and names it for André Messager's comic opera Véronique; tellings differ on the year and the chef, so tell it as a story.

The Redfish Véronique at Brennan's keeps the idea, fish with grapes, with three changes: redfish for sole, a preserved lemon beurre blanc for the creamy sauce, and grapes pickled in hibiscus instead of fresh. Its sauce has left the velouté family for the butter sauces.

Lead with the stock and the finish: a silky sauce of chicken stock and cream, a white wine sauce of fish stock, a velouté brightened with lemon and parsley. Any question about what goes into a sauce goes to the kitchen.

entries.title: The brown family
entries.say: As it reads: the brown family.
entries.summary: The small sauces built on demi-glace: Robert, charcutière, chasseur, diable, piquante, lyonnaise, poivrade, bigarade and the game sauces. Each follows one pattern: an aromatic, an acid reduction, the brown base and a finish.
entries.guest: A brown sauce is a rich, glossy sauce made from roasted bones and wine, given its character by mustard, mushrooms and tarragon, pepper or bitter orange.

paras: The brown family is the set of small sauces made from demi-glace, brown stock and espagnole reduced together until glossy. Demi-glace on its own is deep and meaty but heavy; each daughter cuts it with something sharp and gives it a character. Most classical brown sauces on a menu, in a bistro or a steakhouse, are one of these or a cousin.

Every member follows the same pattern, and a cook who knows it can make any of them from memory: an aromatic cooked in butter, an acid reduced over it, the brown base simmered in, and a finish added at the end. Change one of the four and the sauce changes its name.

Take Robert as the model. Cook a finely chopped onion gently in butter until soft and barely coloured. Add white wine, often with a splash of vinegar, and reduce it by about two-thirds, until the pan is almost syrupy: reduction concentrates the acid and drives off the raw taste of the wine. Add the demi-glace and simmer for about 10 minutes, skimming. Off the heat, whisk in Dijon mustard, and do not let the sauce boil again, or the mustard turns harsh and grainy.

The proportions hold across the family: for 500 ml (about 2 cups) of demi-glace, about 150 ml (2/3 cup) of wine, or wine and vinegar, reduced by two-thirds over two shallots or a small onion. Season at the end, because demi-glace is already concentrated and reduces further as it simmers.

Robert, onion, white wine, demi-glace and mustard, is the old partner of grilled pork. Charcutière, the pork butcher's sauce, is Robert with gherkins (cornichons) cut into fine strips. Chasseur, the hunter's sauce, is sliced mushrooms and shallot sautéed in butter, white wine reduced, tomato and demi-glace, finished with chopped tarragon and parsley: the sauce of chicken chasseur. Diable, the devil's sauce, is white wine and shallot reduced, demi-glace and a good pinch of cayenne, for grilled chicken. The French piquante is vinegar, white wine and shallot reduced, demi-glace, then chopped gherkins and herbs; the Cajun sauce piquante is another dish.

Lyonnaise is onions cooked golden in butter, white wine and vinegar reduced over them, then demi-glace: where Robert keeps the onion pale and adds mustard, lyonnaise browns it and stops. Poivrade, the pepper sauce, starts with a mirepoix browned with game trimmings, then vinegar and the marinade reduced and demi-glace simmered in, with crushed peppercorns added only for the last few minutes. Bigarade, named for the bitter orange, is duck juices or demi-glace with the juice and fine strips of zest of bitter oranges, balanced by a gastrique, sugar cooked to caramel and dissolved with vinegar. It is the sauce of canard à l'orange.

Grand veneur, the master of the hunt's sauce, is the family at its richest: a game poivrade finished with redcurrant jelly and cream, served with venison. The game sauces keep the family's shape with deeper stock, the marinade in the reduction and a sweet or rich finish against the strong meat.

Bitterness comes from a scorched reduction, burnt shallot or pepper simmered too long; strain and soften it with a knob of butter, or start the reduction again. A gluey sauce comes from demi-glace reduced too far or heavy with roux; loosen it with brown stock. Too sharp means the acid was not reduced enough; simmer longer or balance with more demi-glace. Mustard boiled after it goes in turns grainy and harsh.

A guest rarely meets these names, so describe the build: a rich brown sauce of roasted stock and white wine, with mustard, or with mushrooms and tarragon, or with bitter orange for the duck. At Brennan's the brown side shows in the marchand de vin on the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen, a cousin with its own entry. Questions about what a sauce is made with go to the kitchen.

cards.front: How is sauce Robert built?
cards.back: Onion softened in butter, white wine (often with vinegar) reduced, demi-glace simmered in, and Dijon mustard whisked in off the heat.

cards.front: What turns Robert into charcutière?
cards.back: Gherkins, cornichons, cut into fine strips and added at the end: the pork butcher's sauce.

cards.front: What goes into sauce chasseur?
cards.back: Sliced mushrooms and shallot sautéed in butter, white wine reduced, tomato and demi-glace, finished with tarragon and parsley.

cards.front: What defines sauce diable?
cards.back: A white wine and shallot reduction with demi-glace and a good pinch of cayenne: the devil's heat, for grilled chicken.

cards.front: How does the French sauce piquante differ from the Cajun one?
cards.back: The French piquante is demi-glace with vinegar, shallot, gherkins and herbs; the Cajun sauce piquante is a spicy tomato stew, a separate dish.

cards.front: How does lyonnaise differ from sauce Robert?
cards.back: Lyonnaise cooks the onions golden and adds no mustard; Robert keeps them pale and finishes with mustard.

cards.front: When do the crushed peppercorns go into a poivrade, and why?
cards.back: Only for the last few minutes of simmering, so they give heat and aroma without turning the sauce bitter.

cards.front: What is sauce bigarade?
cards.back: Duck juices or demi-glace with bitter orange juice and zest, balanced by a gastrique: the sauce of canard à l'orange.

cards.front: What is a gastrique?
cards.back: Sugar cooked to caramel and dissolved with vinegar, used to balance sweet and sour in sauces such as bigarade.

cards.front: What is sauce grand veneur?
cards.back: The family at its richest: a game poivrade finished with redcurrant jelly and cream, served with venison.

cards.front: Why must sauce Robert not boil after the mustard goes in?
cards.back: Boiling turns mustard harsh and grainy, so it is whisked in off the heat at the very end.

questions.why: The aromatic cooks first, the acid reduces over it, the brown base simmers in, and the finish goes in last, off the heat.

questions.q: Which finish, whisked in off the heat, marks sauce Robert?

questions.q: Charcutière is sauce Robert with what added?
questions.why: Gherkins, cornichons, give the pork butcher's sauce its sharp crunch; marrow belongs to bordelaise and mushrooms to chasseur.

questions.q: Why do the crushed peppercorns go into a poivrade only near the end?

questions.why: Added for the last few minutes, the pepper gives heat and aroma; simmered for long, it leaches bitterness into the sauce.

questions.q: Which sauce is served with canard à l'orange?

entries.title: Madère, Périgueux and the wine-finished sauces
entries.summary: Brown sauces finished with fortified wine: madère, Périgueux and périgourdine with truffle, financière, and the Madeira, port and sherry that finish sauces and soups. The rule: add the wine late and never boil it hard.
entries.guest: Madeira, port and sherry are fortified wines, strengthened with grape spirit. A spoonful added at the end gives a sauce or a soup a nutty, caramel depth.

paras: A fortified wine is wine strengthened with grape spirit: Madeira from the Portuguese island, port from the Douro valley in northern Portugal, sherry from around Jerez in southern Spain. Their sweetness, nuttiness and perfume suit the end of a sauce. Stirred into demi-glace at the last moment, a measure of Madeira turns a meaty base into sauce madère, and the richest brown sauces, Périgueux and its cousins, are built on that.

One rule runs from Escoffier's sauces to a bowl of New Orleans turtle soup: a fortified wine used as a finish goes in late and is never boiled hard, because the perfume a cook pays for is the first thing heat drives off.

For madère, reduce 1 litre (about 1 quart) of demi-glace until it is noticeably thicker than the finished sauce should be, because the wine will thin it. Take the pan off the heat and add about 150 ml (2/3 cup) of Madeira, roughly seven parts base to one of wine. Strain, and hold it hot without letting it boil again. The sauce should be glossy, coat a spoon and smell of the wine, not merely taste of it.

Port and sherry follow the same rule: a ruby or tawny port, a dry amontillado or oloroso sherry, added at the end, tasted and corrected. Where a recipe wants a deeper, sweeter note, a cook may instead reduce the wine first with shallot and then add the base. That is a different sauce, a reduction, and it trades perfume for concentration.

Périgueux, named for the capital of Périgord, the black truffle country of south-west France, is madère with truffle essence, the liquor of cooked truffles, and chopped black truffle. Périgourdine is the same sauce with the truffle in slices or shaped into small balls, and some texts add foie gras. Financière, the financier's sauce, is a Madeira sauce made richer with truffle; it dressed an old garnish of chicken quenelles, mushrooms and truffle served in a vol-au-vent, a puff pastry case. All three are madère first, and the truffle is the finish.

A glaze is the exception to the rule. Reduce the wine with butter or stock until it is syrupy and clings to a vegetable or a piece of meat, sweet and savoury at once: the perfume softens, and the caramel and walnut of Madeira come forward.

Brennan's carries both uses. Aged sherry finishes the Turtle Soup, with brown butter spinach and grated egg: a spoonful of nutty, dry sherry lifts the rich, dark soup the way lemon lifts fish. In some New Orleans dining rooms sherry also comes to the table in a small jug or cruet for the guest to add; whether Brennan's adds it in the kitchen, at the pass or at the table is a question for lineup.

On the dinner Creole Hanger Steak, broccolini is glazed with Madeira, the wine reduced until syrupy, a sweet, nutty counterweight to the Creole spice and chilli crisp. Neither bottle is named in the house notes, so never promise a producer, and tell every guest who avoids alcohol that the wine is there; never promise it has cooked off.

Truffle words on a menu promise different things. Fresh black truffle, Tuber melanosporum, from Périgord and elsewhere, is a winter tuber, in season roughly December to March; the summer truffle looks similar and tastes milder. Truffle essence and truffle juice come from cooked truffles. Much truffle oil, and some truffle butter and salt, is flavoured with a made aroma rather than truffle itself. Which of these is on a plate is a question for the kitchen, and the guest should hear the plain answer.

Say it simply: a rich brown sauce finished with Madeira, a fortified wine that tastes of caramel and walnut; with truffle, the black truffle of Périgord. For the turtle soup: finished with aged sherry from Jerez, nutty and dry, which cuts the richness.

entries.title: The hollandaise and béarnaise families
entries.summary: The daughters of hollandaise and béarnaise: mousseline, maltaise, Mikado, noisette and moutarde on one side, Paloise, Choron and Foyot on the other. Each is acid, yolks and butter with one defining addition.
entries.guest: These are warm butter sauces thickened with egg yolk, each with one extra note: whipped cream, blood orange, brown butter, mustard, mint, tomato or a reduced meat glaze.

paras: Hollandaise and béarnaise are the two warm emulsions of the classical kitchen: egg yolks holding warm butter in fine droplets, sharpened with acid. Hollandaise takes lemon or a plain vinegar reduction; béarnaise is built on a reduction of white wine, tarragon vinegar, shallot and herbs. From each comes a family, and the rule that governs it is short: an acid, yolks, butter, then one defining addition. Know the addition and you know the sauce.

Because the base is the same, so are the dangers. Every daughter scrambles if it overheats and splits if the butter goes in too fast, and each addition brings a risk of its own: water from juice, weight from cream, heat from brown butter.

Make the mother first, then add. Whisk the yolks with the reduction over barely simmering water to a thick ribbon, about 65°C (149°F), mount the warm butter off the heat and season. Only then does the defining addition go in, and how it goes in matters.

Folded additions go in last and gently: whipped cream for mousseline, just before the plate leaves. Liquid additions are reduced first, so they flavour without thinning: blood orange or mandarin juice cooked down by half, then whisked in with fine zest. Butter additions replace the plain butter: for noisette, cook the butter until the milk solids brown and it smells of hazelnut, then let it cool to warm, about 60°C (140°F), before it meets the yolks. Herb additions are split between the reduction and the finish: mint stalks in the vinegar for Paloise, chopped mint at the end.

Mousseline, also called Chantilly, is hollandaise with lightly whipped cream folded in, about one part cream to three or four of sauce: lighter, paler and softer, for poached fish and asparagus. Maltaise is hollandaise with blood orange juice and grated zest, named for the blood oranges of Malta, and the classic sauce for asparagus. Mikado does the same with mandarin. Noisette is hollandaise made with brown butter, beurre noisette, darker and nutty in taste; the name describes the butter's colour. Moutarde is hollandaise finished with Dijon mustard, sharp enough for grilled fish.

Paloise, named for Pau, the old capital of Béarn, is béarnaise with mint in place of tarragon, in the reduction and the finish, for lamb. Choron is béarnaise with tomato cooked down to a thick paste. Foyot is béarnaise with glace de viande, reduced meat glaze, whisked in, tawny and deep, and many texts call the same sauce Valois; both have an entry of their own. Further out sit rare names such as Arlésienne and Tyrolienne, which the old books record and describe differently; they show how far the family runs.

Too much juice in a maltaise or Mikado thins the sauce and can split it, so reduce the juice first. Cream folded in too early collapses in the heat and leaves a mousseline loose and greasy; fold it in at the pass. Brown butter added hot scrambles the yolks, and butter taken too dark turns a noisette bitter; cool it to warm and stop at hazelnut brown. Mint chopped long before service blackens and loses its scent. For a split or scrambled base, the rescue is the hollandaise rescue, taught with breaking and rescuing.

The house's own notes read the menu as a lesson in this family: plain hollandaise on the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen, béarnaise on the breakfast Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak, Choron on the Eggs Sardou and Foyot on the Roasted Chateaubriand. A server who knows the family can describe all four sauces from one idea.

Describe the base, then the addition: a warm butter sauce thickened with egg yolk, with blood orange, or lightened with whipped cream, or with mint for lamb. The name noisette comes from the colour of browned butter; whether a sauce carries nuts, egg or anything else a guest asks about is a question for the kitchen.

entries.title: Reading the sauce tree
entries.say: As it reads: reading the sauce tree.
entries.summary: Every classical sauce is a mother, a defining addition and a finish. Learn to read a sauce's name as directions, to a place, a person or a garnish, and any French sauce on any menu becomes something you can explain.
entries.guest: Every French sauce name is a small map. Choron, on the Eggs Sardou, is béarnaise with tomato, named for a Paris chef, Alexandre Choron.

paras: The sauce tree is a way of reading. Every classical French sauce is built in three layers: a mother, a defining addition and a finish. The mother is one of the five bases a kitchen keeps ready: béchamel, velouté, espagnole (usually as demi-glace, its reduced and refined form), tomate or hollandaise. The addition makes the sauce itself: a flavour such as wine, a garnish such as mushrooms, or an enrichment such as cream or cheese. The finish is the last touch at the pass: butter, herbs, the final seasoning.

Put the layers together and the name follows. Bordelaise is demi-glace with a red wine and shallot reduction, finished with bone marrow. Mornay is béchamel with cheese. A Chef reads the tree both ways: from build to name, and from name back to build.

A place name promises an ingredient. Bordelaise points to Bordeaux and its red wine. Lyonnaise points to Lyon, whose cooking is known for onions. Normande points to Normandy's cream and cider: the classical fish sauce carries the cream, while cider belongs to homelier dishes cooked à la normande. Nantua, a town in the Ain, was known for its crayfish, so sauce Nantua carries crayfish butter and tails. Périgueux is the capital of Périgord, the black truffle country, so its sauce is Madeira demi-glace with chopped truffle.

Béarnaise is the exception that teaches. It is named for Béarn, the home region of King Henri IV, but tradition credits it to the chef Collinet, said to have made it in 1836 for the opening of the Pavillon Henri IV at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, near Paris. A place name promises character, not always a birthplace.

Other names honour people, and a Chef keeps record and legend apart. Choron's namesake is on record: Alexandre Étienne Choron was chef de cuisine at Voisin, a celebrated Paris restaurant, though whether he created the sauce is not recorded. Foyot takes its name from the Restaurant Foyot on the rue de Tournon. Soubise is said to honour Charles de Rohan, prince de Soubise, an eighteenth-century marshal of France, though nobody can show that his cooks made it.

Mornay is the cautionary tale. It is often said to honour Philippe de Mornay, a Protestant statesman who died in 1623, yet no recipe of that name is known before the nineteenth century. Cooks named dishes to flatter a patron, and stories grew afterwards: a name is a dedication, not always a record.

To read a name backwards, take three steps. Find the mother: brown, white, tomato, or yolk and butter. Find the addition the name promises: a place, a person whose sauce you have learnt, or a plain word. Then ask how it is finished. Chasseur is French for hunter, so think of the hunter's woods: sliced mushrooms and shallot sautéed in butter, white wine reduced over them, tomato and demi-glace, finished with tarragon and parsley.

Not every sauce sits on the tree. Beurre blanc is butter alone, whisked into a reduction of wine, vinegar and shallot, with no roux and no yolk. A pan sauce is built to order from the browned juices in the pan. The Creole sauces sit at the tree's edge as cousins of sauce tomate: they share its tomato but start from the holy trinity of onion, celery and bell pepper, with cayenne, and follow their own logic. The New Orleans bordelaise, usually a garlic butter with olive oil and parsley, shares a name with the French red wine sauce and little else.

The Brennan's menu shows both halves. Choron on the Eggs Sardou and Foyot on the Roasted Chateaubriand read down the hollandaise branch, through béarnaise. The Creole sauce on the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits sits at the edge of the tree, a cousin of sauce tomate. The pecan bordelaise on the Pecan Gulf Fish sits outside it, and the house notes call that bordelaise a reading, not a recipe: confirm with the kitchen which one it is before you pair a wine.

Knowing the tree, a server can describe any sauce in three parts: the base, the addition and how it eats. Soubise is a creamy white sauce with sweet, slow-cooked onion; chasseur is a rich brown sauce with mushrooms, a little tomato and tarragon. When a name is new to you, ask the kitchen rather than guess, because names drift. Questions about what a sauce carries, from flour to shellfish, go to the kitchen too.

brennans.how: Choron reads straight down the hollandaise branch: yolk and butter, then béarnaise's tarragon reduction, then tomato cooked down to a paste. On the Eggs Sardou it takes the place of hollandaise; say béarnaise with tomato, tangy and herbal.

The name is French, but the sauce most likely belongs to the New Orleans garlic butter family, with toasted pecans. The house notes call that a reading, not a recipe: confirm with the kitchen which bordelaise it is before pairing wine.

Creole sauce stands at the edge of the French tree, a cousin of sauce tomate: the holy trinity softened with garlic, then tomato, stock, bay, thyme and cayenne. On the Shrimp & Grits it carries tasso, a spiced, smoked Louisiana pork, so it is smoky as well as tangy.
