cards.back: Beurre blanc (butter alone, whisked into a reduction), pan sauces built from the browned juices in the pan and the New Orleans bordelaise; the Creole sauces stand at the edge, cousins of sauce tomate.

cards.front: What does bordelaise usually mean in a New Orleans restaurant?
cards.back: A garlic butter, butter and olive oil with garlic and parsley, not the French red wine sauce with marrow. Confirm with the kitchen which one a dish carries.

cards.front: How does a server describe an unfamiliar classical sauce?
cards.back: Base, addition, then how it eats: Soubise is a creamy white sauce with sweet, slow-cooked onion. If the name is new to you, ask the kitchen rather than guess.

cards.front: Which Brennan's dish carries Choron, and how do you read it?
cards.back: The Eggs Sardou: hollandaise, then béarnaise's tarragon reduction, then tomato cooked to a paste. Foyot on the Chateaubriand reads the same branch, with meat glaze in place of tomato.

questions.q: Which three layers build every classical sauce on the sauce tree?
questions.answer: A mother, an addition and a finish
distractors: A stock, a starch thickener and a garnish
A roux, a wine and a herb
A fat, an acid and a salt
questions.why: Every classical sauce starts from one of the mothers, takes the addition that names it, and is finished at the pass with butter, herbs or seasoning.

questions.q: A sauce named Nantua promises which ingredient?
questions.why: Nantua, a town in the Ain, was known for its crayfish; truffle points to Périgueux, red wine to Bordeaux and onions to Lyon.

questions.q: Béarnaise is named for Béarn. Where, by tradition, was it first made?
distractors: In Pau, the capital of Béarn
In Bordeaux, for a banquet of wine merchants
In Lyon, for a guild banquet
questions.why: Tradition credits Collinet at the Pavillon Henri IV in 1836; the name honours Henri IV's home region, so a place name promises character, not a birthplace.

questions.q: Why is the story that sauce Mornay honours Philippe de Mornay doubted?
questions.answer: No such recipe is known before the 1800s
distractors: He was chef at a rival Paris restaurant
Mornay is an old French word for cheese
He is known to have refused all sauces
questions.why: Philippe de Mornay died in 1623 and the sauce appears in the nineteenth century, so the name reads as a dedication, not a record.

questions.q: Reading the name backwards, which garnish defines sauce chasseur?
questions.why: Chasseur is the hunter's sauce: mushrooms and shallot in butter, white wine, tomato and demi-glace, finished with tarragon. Marrow is bordelaise and crayfish is Nantua.

questions.q: Which of these sauces sits outside the classical sauce tree?
questions.why: Beurre blanc is butter whisked into a reduction with no mother beneath it; chasseur and French bordelaise come from demi-glace, and Mornay from béchamel.

questions.q: What does the name of the classical sauce normande promise?
questions.why: Normandy is cream country, so the classical fish sauce normande is enriched with cream and yolks; cider belongs to homelier dishes cooked à la normande.

questions.q: A guest asks what Soubise is. Which answer reads the tree correctly?
questions.answer: A creamy white sauce with sweet onion
distractors: A brown sauce with red wine and shallot
A buttery yolk sauce with tarragon
A tomato sauce with peppers and cayenne
questions.why: Name the base, then the addition, then how it eats: Soubise is béchamel with a purée of onions cooked soft and sweet.

questions.q: The Foyot on the Roasted Chateaubriand carries meat glaze. Which branch of the tree does it read down?
questions.why: Foyot is béarnaise with glace de viande whisked in; the glaze comes from the brown side, but the sauce is a yolk and butter emulsion, so it reads down the hollandaise branch.

entries.title: Finishing a sauce
entries.say: As it reads: finishing a sauce.
entries.summary: Everything a cook does between a sauce that is cooked and a sauce that is ready: reducing it to nappe, skimming, passing it through a fine sieve, protecting its surface, holding it at the right heat and tasting it last.
entries.guest: Classic French sauces are finished at the last moment: strained smooth, seasoned, often given a piece of butter for shine, and tasted before they go out.

paras: Finishing is the work between a sauce that is cooked and a sauce that is ready for the plate. The base may be right, but a sauce goes out only when it has the right body, a clean surface, a smooth texture and a seasoning tasted at the last moment. Finishing is where a good sauce becomes the kitchen's sauce, and where most faults are caught or missed.

The words are French because the method is: nappe, dépouiller, passer, tamponner. Each names one small job, and together they make the routine a saucier, the cook in charge of sauces, follows every service.

Start with body. Reduce the sauce at a steady simmer until it is nappe, from the French for tablecloth: it coats the back of a spoon in an even layer, and a finger drawn across leaves a clean line that does not run back together. Thinner, and it pools on the plate; thicker, and it sits like paste. Taste as it reduces, but hold back the salt, because reduction concentrates it.

Keep it clean while it simmers. To dépouiller, literally to skin, set the pan half off the heat so the sauce bubbles on one side only. The movement pushes fat and scum to the still side, where they gather to be lifted off with a ladle every few minutes. A long-simmered velouté or espagnole is skimmed this way for an hour or more.

Pass it. A chinois, a fine conical strainer named for its likeness to a Chinese hat, takes out lumps, shallot and herbs: ladle the sauce in and tap the rim or press gently with the back of the ladle, never forcing the solids through, which clouds the sauce. The finest sauces go further, through a tamis, a flat drum sieve, or an étamine, a square of fine cloth the old kitchens wrung between two cooks.

Then the last adjustment, over low heat or off it. Salt in small pinches. A few drops of lemon juice or vinegar to wake a rich sauce. A splash of wine, cream or Madeira for the sauces that call for it, added late so its scent is not boiled away. A piece of cold butter swirled in for gloss, the step called monter au beurre, which has its own entry. Then taste once more, with a clean spoon.

If the sauce must wait, tamponner it: dot the surface with small pieces of butter, which melt into a film that stops a skin forming, or lay a disc of buttered paper on top. Hold each family at its own heat in a bain-marie, a pan of hot water. Brown sauces and the roux-thickened white sauces sit hot, around 80°C (176°F), and never below 57°C (135°F), the hot holding line in the FDA Food Code. Warm emulsions such as hollandaise sit warm, about 60°C (140°F), because more heat splits them; their holding rules have their own entry.

A skin means the sauce waited uncovered: lift it off, pass the sauce again and tamponner it. Beads of fat on top mean it was not skimmed: dépouiller it, or draw a strip of kitchen paper across the surface. Lumps go through the chinois. A sauce reduced too far is loosened with a little of its own stock, and one that tastes too salty after reduction can take unsalted stock or cream, but the lasting cure is to season at the end.

A server meets the finish without seeing it: the gloss on the plate, a sauce that holds its line instead of running. Carry sauced plates straight from the pass, because a sauce that cools thickens and dulls, and send a sauce on the side out in a warmed boat. If a guest finds a sauce too salty or with a skin on it, take it back to the kitchen rather than defend it at the table, and send any question about the butter or cream in a finish to the kitchen as well.

faults.cause: The sauce waited uncovered and its surface dried.
faults.fix: Lift the skin off, pass the sauce again, then dot it with butter or cover it with buttered paper.

faults.cause: It was not skimmed while it simmered.
faults.fix: Simmer it off centre and skim the still side, or draw kitchen paper across the surface.

faults.cause: It was not passed, or the roux was not whisked smooth into the liquid.
faults.fix: Pass it through a chinois, pressing gently with the ladle; for the finest sauces, pass it twice.

faults.cause: It was not reduced to nappe.
faults.fix: Simmer on, skimming, until it coats the spoon and a finger leaves a clean line.

faults.cause: It was seasoned before reduction concentrated the salt.
faults.fix: Loosen it with unsalted stock or cream, and season at the end next time.

faults.cause: It lacks salt or acid at the finish.
faults.fix: Add salt in small pinches and a few drops of lemon juice or vinegar, then taste again.

cards.front: What does nappe mean, and how do you test for it?
cards.back: The sauce coats the back of a spoon in an even layer, and a finger drawn across leaves a clean line that does not run back together.

cards.front: What is dépouiller, and why set the pan off centre?
cards.back: Skimming a simmering sauce: half off the heat, it bubbles on one side only, which pushes fat and scum to the still side to be lifted off.

cards.front: What is a chinois, and how is a sauce passed through it?
cards.back: A fine conical strainer. Ladle the sauce in and tap the rim or press gently with the ladle; forcing the solids through clouds the sauce.

cards.front: When would a cook reach for a tamis or an étamine?
cards.back: For the finest sauces: a tamis is a flat drum sieve and an étamine a square of fine cloth, and both catch what a chinois lets through.

cards.front: What is tamponner, and what problem does it solve?
cards.back: Dotting the surface of a waiting sauce with small pieces of butter, which melt into a film that stops a skin forming.

cards.front: How are brown sauces held through service?
cards.back: Hot in a bain-marie, around 80°C (176°F), covered or buttered, and never below 57°C (135°F), the hot holding line in the FDA Food Code.

cards.front: Why are warm emulsions held warm rather than hot?
cards.back: More heat splits them or sets the yolk, so they wait at about 60°C (140°F), away from direct heat, under their own holding rules.

cards.front: Why is salt adjusted at the end of a sauce, not the start?
cards.back: Reduction concentrates salt along with flavour, so a sauce seasoned early can end too salty once it has reduced to nappe.

cards.front: What do a few drops of lemon juice or vinegar do at the finish?
cards.back: They sharpen and brighten a rich sauce so its flavours read clearly; added at the end, their freshness is not cooked away.

cards.front: Why does a splash of Madeira or wine go in at the very end?
cards.back: Boiling drives off its scent, so it goes in late, off the boil, and the sauce keeps the aroma it is named for.

cards.front: A sauce has formed a skin in the bain-marie. What do you do?
cards.back: Lift the skin off, pass the sauce again through the chinois, then dot it with butter or cover it with buttered paper so no new skin forms.

questions.q: A finger drawn across a sauce-coated spoon leaves a clean line. What has the sauce reached?
questions.why: Nappe means the sauce coats the spoon evenly and holds a clean line; a glace is a far heavier reduction of stock, and a ribbon is whisked yolk.

questions.q: Why does a cook set a simmering sauce half off the burner while it reduces?
questions.answer: To gather fat and scum for skimming
distractors: To stop the sauce reducing at all
To cook the roux a shade darker
To let the sauce caramelise evenly
questions.why: Bubbling on one side only drives fat and impurities across to the calm side, where the cook lifts them off: that is dépouiller.

questions.q: What does it mean to tamponner a sauce that must wait?
distractors: Strain it twice through a cloth
Whisk in egg yolk off the heat
Stir it with a flat wooden spoon
questions.why: The butter melts into a thin film over the sauce, so the surface cannot dry into a skin while it sits in the bain-marie.

questions.q: Which tool gives the finest finish, catching what a chinois lets through?
distractors: A food mill on its finest plate
questions.why: A sauce wrung or passed through fine cloth leaves behind particles a metal strainer misses; a colander, a food mill and a perforated china cap are all coarser.

questions.q: Below what temperature should a sauce held hot never fall, by the FDA Food Code?
questions.why: The Food Code sets 57°C (135°F) as the hot holding line; brown sauces sit well above it, around 80°C (176°F), in the bain-marie.

questions.q: Why is a hollandaise held warm, at about 60°C (140°F), rather than hot?
questions.answer: Heat splits it or sets the yolk
distractors: Its lemon turns bitter when hot
It loses its colour when hot
It can no longer be strained
questions.why: A warm emulsion depends on gentle heat: too hot and the fat separates or the yolk proteins set, so it waits warm, away from direct heat.

questions.q: Why should a sauce be salted to taste at the end rather than the start?
distractors: Salt dissolves only in cold sauces
Salt turns a brown sauce grey
questions.why: As water simmers away, the salt stays behind, so a sauce seasoned early can be too salty by the time it reaches nappe.

questions.q: What do a few drops of lemon juice do to a rich finished sauce?
distractors: Thicken it until it coats a spoon
Stop a skin forming on top
questions.why: Acid cuts through richness so the flavours read clearly; it goes in at the end so its freshness is not cooked away.

entries.title: The sauces in Le Guide culinaire
entries.summary: How Escoffier ordered the sauce chapter of Le Guide culinaire (1903): four great base sauces with their working bases, then the small sauces, English sauces, cold sauces and compound butters, and how to read the old text today.
entries.guest: Escoffier's Le Guide culinaire of 1903 set down the classic French sauces, among them the hollandaise and béarnaise on our egg dishes and steaks.

paras: Le Guide culinaire is Auguste Escoffier's handbook of the professional French kitchen, first published in Paris in 1903 and written with Philéas Gilbert and Émile Fétu. Its subtitle, aide-mémoire de cuisine pratique, means a memory aid for practical cooking: it was written for cooks who already knew their trade, thousands of numbered preparations set down briefly so a brigade could make each one the same way every service.
The sauce chapter is its backbone. Nearly every dish in the book ends with a sauce named there, so knowing how that chapter is built is knowing how the classical repertoire fits together.

The book opens with the fonds de cuisine, the kitchen's foundations: the stocks, the glazes made by reducing them, and the roux that thicken them. The grandes sauces de base, the great base sauces, come next. The small sauces built on them follow, the small compound brown sauces and then the white. After them come the English sauces, the cold sauces, mayonnaise among them, and the compound butters, butter worked with a flavouring to finish a sauce or a grill.

Escoffier built on Carême, who had sorted sauces into families early in the nineteenth century, and trimmed him. He wanted sauces lighter and quicker to finish, and plates with fewer garnishes, the towering decoration of the grand style left behind. He wrote for a restaurant brigade cooking to order, where a sauce had to be ready at the pass in minutes, so the bases are made ahead and each small sauce is a short step from one of them.

The French text names four grandes sauces de base: espagnole, velouté, béchamel and tomate. Beside them, under the same heading, stand the working bases a cook draws on: demi-glace, espagnole reduced and refined; jus lié, veal stock thickened, usually with arrowroot; allemande, velouté bound with egg yolk; and the chicken and fish veloutés. Hollandaise and béarnaise, the warm sauces of yolk and butter, are not base sauces in the French book. They appear among the small compound sauces, entries in the run rather than heads of a family.

Read the Guide with the edition in hand. Escoffier revised it through four French editions, in 1903, 1907, 1912 and 1921, adding, cutting and renumbering as he went, so a list or a recipe number from one may not match another. The English translation of 1907, A Guide to Modern Cookery, is abridged and calls the base sauces the leading sauces. Its chapter of leading warm sauces also prints hollandaise, where the French book had set it among the small sauces, and many trace the familiar five to that page. The complete English translation, by H. L. Cracknell and R. J. Kaufmann (1979), follows the fourth edition.

Use the Guide as a record of a repertoire, not a recipe to copy line by line. Its quantities suit large batches, its methods assume a trained hand, and its stocks assume hours and veal bones a modern kitchen may not give. What it records without fail is what each sauce was, what it was built on and what its name promised, and that is the knowledge to carry into a kitchen cooking today.

On the floor the Guide settles a common table conversation. A guest who says Escoffier gave us five mother sauces is half right: his French book named four base sauces, and the five came with the teaching that followed. Say so lightly, as a story worth telling, never as a correction. When a menu calls a sauce classical, the Guide is usually what that word points to.

distractors: Milk thickened with a white roux
questions.why: Jus lié is the light brown base of thickened veal stock; allemande is velouté with yolk, demi-glace is refined espagnole, and milk with roux is béchamel.

questions.q: What comes first in Le Guide culinaire, before any sauce?
questions.why: The fonds de cuisine come first because every base sauce is built from a stock and most are thickened with a roux.

distractors: Among the cold sauces, after mayonnaise
In the chapter on egg dishes

questions.q: A guest says Escoffier named five mother sauces. What is the accurate reply?
questions.answer: His French book named four base sauces
distractors: He named seven, mayonnaise among them
He named three: brown, white and red

steps.title: Build a hollandaise
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a classic hollandaise in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Reduce white wine vinegar with crushed white peppercorns and a little water, then strain it and let it cool
While the reduction cools, clarify the butter and keep it warm, not hot
Whisk the yolks with the reduction in a bowl over barely simmering water, the bowl never touching it
Keep whisking until the yolks thicken into a pale ribbon, at about 60 to 65°C (140 to 149°F)
Off the heat, whisk in the warm butter a few drops at a time until it takes, then in a thin stream
Season with salt, lemon juice and a pinch of cayenne, loosening it with warm water if it stiffens
Hold it warm, around 60°C (140°F), in a bain-marie away from direct heat
steps.distractor: Bring the yolks to a rolling boil so they thicken faster
steps.why: The reduction is made and cooled, and the butter clarified, before the yolks meet any heat. The yolks are taken to a ribbon over gentle heat, and only then does the butter go in, slowly and off the heat; the finished sauce is held warm, never hot.

steps.title: Make a béchamel
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a classic béchamel in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Pin a bay leaf to half an onion with a clove, warm it in the milk to infuse, then lift it out
With the milk infused, melt the butter over a low heat and stir in an equal weight of flour
Cook the roux for 2 to 3 minutes, stirring, until it smells of biscuit but shows no colour
Add the warm milk in three or four stages, whisking each one smooth before the next
Keep whisking as it comes up to a bare simmer and thickens
Simmer it gently for at least 15 to 20 minutes, stirring the corners, until no floury taste remains
Season with salt, white pepper and nutmeg, and strain it through a fine sieve
Press parchment onto the surface and hold it in a bain-marie at 57°C (135°F) or above
steps.distractor: Cook the roux until it turns the colour of milky coffee
steps.why: The milk takes the onion's flavour before it meets the roux, and the white roux cooks without colour. The milk goes in by stages so the starch spreads before it swells, the long gentle simmer cooks out the flour, and seasoning, straining and a covered surface come last.

steps.title: Make a velouté
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a classic velouté in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Melt the butter and stir in an equal weight of flour
Cook the roux over a low to moderate heat for 3 to 5 minutes, until pale gold and nutty
Take the roux off the heat and let it cool for a minute
Whisk in the hot white stock a ladle at a time, smooth after each
Bring it to the boil, still whisking, then lower it to a gentle simmer
Simmer it off centre for at least 30 minutes, skimming fat and scum from the quiet side
Strain it through a fine sieve, season it and protect the surface from a skin
steps.distractor: Roast the bones dark brown first so the stock carries more colour
steps.why: A blond roux, cooled a little, takes hot stock in stages without lumps. The long simmer with the pan off centre gathers fat and scum on one side to be skimmed away, dépouiller, which makes it glossy; salt waits because the sauce concentrates.

steps.title: Make an espagnole
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a classic espagnole in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Brown the mirepoix, with diced bacon or ham if used, in fat over a moderate heat
Stir in the flour and cook it for 8 to 15 minutes, to a hazelnut brown roux
Whisk in the hot brown stock in stages, smooth after each
With the stock whisked in smooth, add the tomato and a bouquet garni and bring it to the boil
Lower it to a lazy simmer, off centre, for two to three hours or more, skimming steadily
Strain it through a fine sieve, pressing lightly
Cool it quickly if it is not used at once
steps.distractor: Salt it fully at the start so the seasoning cooks in
steps.why: Colour comes first, from browned mirepoix and a roux taken to hazelnut, before any liquid goes in. The stock follows in stages, then the tomato and herbs, and hours of off centre simmering and skimming give depth and gloss. Salt waits, because the reduction concentrates it.

steps.title: Take espagnole to demi-glace
steps.prompt: Put the stages of taking espagnole to demi-glace in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Combine equal parts espagnole and brown stock in a heavy pan
Bring it to a simmer with the pan set slightly off centre
Reduce it slowly by about half, skimming the quiet side every 10 to 15 minutes, until it is glossy and coats a spoon
Pass it through a chinois lined with muslin
Off the heat, once strained, finish it with Madeira or dry sherry
Hold it at 57°C (135°F) or above for service, or cool it quickly and chill it
steps.distractor: Boil it hard so it reduces faster
steps.why: Demi-glace is espagnole and brown stock reduced together by half. A gentle simmer with the pan off centre lets the fat be skimmed rather than beaten in, the sauce is strained fine, and the wine goes in last, off the heat, so its perfume survives.

steps.title: The béarnaise reduction
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a béarnaise, from its reduction to the finish, in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Chop the shallots finely and crush the peppercorns
Put the white wine, tarragon vinegar, shallot, tarragon stalks, chervil and pepper in a small pan
Boil it down to about 30 ml (2 tbsp), almost dry and fiercely sharp
Let it cool a little, then strain it, or leave the shallot in for texture
Whisk it with the yolks over barely simmering water until they thicken to a ribbon
Off the heat, mount the warm butter in, slowly at first
Finish with chopped fresh tarragon and chervil, and taste for salt
steps.distractor: Finish it with dried tarragon in place of fresh
steps.why: The reduction is the flavour, so it is boiled almost dry: the acid concentrates and the water that would slacken the sauce is gone. It cools a little before it meets the yolks, the butter goes in off the heat, and the fresh herbs wait for the end.

steps.title: Finish a béarnaise as Choron
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a sauce Choron in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Cook chopped ripe tomatoes in a wide pan, stirring often, until a spoon drawn through leaves a clear line
Pass the tomato through a fine sieve and let it cool to warm
With the tomato ready, reduce the white wine, tarragon vinegar, shallot and tarragon almost dry
Whisk the yolks with the reduction over barely simmering water to a ribbon
Off the heat, mount the warm butter, slowly at first
Fold the warm tomato through the béarnaise, about one part to six
Hold it warm, around 60°C (140°F), in a bain-marie, never on direct heat
steps.distractor: Stir in chopped raw tomato straight from the fridge
steps.why: The tomato is cooked down first, because water is the one thing a yolk and butter sauce cannot spare, and a finished béarnaise will not wait while tomato reduces. The tomato goes in warm and last, off the heat, and the sauce is held warm, never hot.

steps.title: Build a New Orleans marchand de vin
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a New Orleans marchand de vin in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Cook the onion, garlic, ham and mushrooms in butter until soft and lightly browned
Stir in the flour and cook it for 5 to 8 minutes, until it smells nutty and turns light brown
Pour in the red wine and boil it down by half
Add the beef stock, a bay leaf and a sprig of thyme
Simmer it gently for 20 to 30 minutes, skimming, until it coats the back of a spoon
Lift out the herbs and season with salt, black pepper and a pinch of cayenne
steps.distractor: Add the wine and the stock together so they reduce as one
steps.why: The aromatics and ham are browned before the flour goes in, and the roux is cooked before any liquid. The wine is reduced on its own first, to drive off its raw edge, then the stock goes in and the sauce simmers to coating body.
